extracted.intended_audience: citizens/voters and framers debating the design of the national Executive (readers of The Federalist; informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for designing the national executive in a republican constitution (features such as unity, duration, powers, accountability, and appointment authority). The page articulates what qualities an effective and safe Executive ought to have and what institutional forms to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy in the Executive is a leading character of good government; essential for protection against foreign attacks, steady administration of the laws, protection of property, and security of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton lists energy as necessary and then identifies its constituent ingredients. An energetic Executive is contrasted with a 'feeble Executive' which implies bad execution and bad government in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients constituting Executive energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four elements should be combined to produce an Executive capable of decisive and effective administration. Each ingredient is discussed separately in the text to show how it contributes to overall energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity (a single Executive) is conducive to decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch; the fewer the number, the more pronounced these qualities become.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity may be destroyed by having multiple magistrates of equal authority or by having one ostensible chief constrained by a council. Multiplicity reduces decisiveness and makes the executive less effective in crises (e.g., war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of plural/multiplex executive (councils)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plurality of persons in the Executive or a council that shares or controls the ostensible Executive tends to produce dissension, embittered factions, weakened authority, and impeded measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils often become clogs on good intentions, instruments of bad intentions, and a cloak for faults. Examples from state experience and Roman history are used to show dangers; a council appropriate to a perpetual monarch is inappropriate in a republic because it dilutes personal responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive should be constructed so that responsibility for actions is clear—so the public can censure or punish maladministration; plurality tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility has two aspects—censure and punishment—with censure most important in elective offices. Multiplication of the Executive makes detection of misconduct difficult, allows shifting blame ('I was overruled by my council'), and leaves public opinion in suspense about the real author of measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of plurality and risk of collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of executives (e.g., six to a dozen) can combine interest and influence and thus be as dangerous as a single ambitious man with consolidated power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers must be so great as to render combination difficult to secure the supposed safety; otherwise, the united credit and influence of several individuals may be more formidable to liberty than one person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost/expense consideration of a council
rubrics_metrics.description: A council sufficiently numerous to achieve the intended object would require salaries and residence at the seat of government, increasing public expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expense is an additional disadvantage of a plural executive and may outweigh doubtful utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety in the republican sense (two ingredients)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people; secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety must be balanced with energy; dependence on the people and personal responsibility of magistrates are core republican safeguards against abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence from the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The partition of powers should render the Executive independent of the legislature; it must be subordinate to the laws but not dependent on the legislative body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Executive is dependent on the legislature (e.g., too short tenure or removable at will), separation of powers is nominal and the legislative branch may absorb other powers. Executive duration and constitutional protections are means to secure independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration in office to secure firmness and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration in office affects the personal firmness of the magistrate in using constitutional powers and the stability of the administrative system; longer duration increases the probability of firmness and independent action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very short terms produce feebleness and irresolution because the incumbent has little vested interest; a limited but substantial term (Hamilton argues four years as contributing materially) gives time to establish reputation and act with independent judgment, while not creating undue danger to liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between duration and accountability (term length)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term length should be long enough to create firmness and a stake in office but short enough to preserve accountability to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton reasons that no limited duration will be perfect, but a four-year term contributes materially to firmness without justifying alarm for public liberty; it provides a middle ground between independence and electoral check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to popular and legislative fashion (executive courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive should be able to resist transient popular impulses and legislative fashions when those oppose the public good; duration and firmness enable the magistrate to withstand temporary delusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public commonly intend the public good but may err about means; a chief magistrate with some independence can provide time for reflection and protect long-term public interest from passing enthusiasms or manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and supervision of executive administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who manage the administration (foreign negotiations, finance, armed forces, disbursement) ought to be assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate, derive their offices from his nomination, and be subject to his superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links the duration and stability of the chief magistrate to continuity in administration; a chief must have appointment authority to ensure coherent execution of policy and to prevent a successor from undoing an administration’s measures purely for display of capacity.
